zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Review aid (not transcribed): The supplied page subset of Entry Words Data of Nippojisho was consulted after an independent scan reading for lexical identification and coverage. NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The returned transcription choices and English line notes are this reviewer’s scan-based work, not a copied NINJAL transcription.

lines.note: Uo vtçu completes Go at the foot of f242: playing the board game. The cedilla in vtçu and the space in eſte jogo are visible; the previous page’s isolated uo is a catchword, not a second occurrence in the running definition.

runs.text: Nome de certa parte do reino, ou co-

lines.note: Gǒ names a territorial subdivision of a kingdom. The caron is visible; co- begins comarca in the next physical line.
Marca completes co-marca, a district. This short continuation closes the territorial sense and is not part of the following measure entry.
A separate Gǒ is a measure used for rice and other substances. The printed caron and the unexpanded &c. are retained.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Medidaſinha com que medem Cha

lines.note: Item adds a small measure used for tea and other materials. Medidaſinha is the printed diminutive; Cha belongs to the Portuguese explanation of what is measured.
Moido qualifies the tea in the preceding line as ground or powdered, followed by medicines. The scan has moido, not the draft’s mordo; no extra r is present.

runs.text: Certa tinta que ſe faz de feijoẽs moidos

lines.note: Go is a preparation described as a dye made from ground beans. The tilde in feijoẽs is over e, and the historical spelling moidos is preserved.

runs.text: com outras couſas pera tingir, & fazer que ſe

lines.note: Other ingredients are added for dyeing and for making the other colors resist fading. The purpose clause continues into the next physical line.
Não desbotem states that the other dyes should not fade. The visible ascender belongs to b, restoring desbotem rather than the draft’s broken des otem.
Gǒacu, explained by Tçuyoi acu, means great wickedness. The final Portuguese alternative follows below; the accent is not expanded into a modern spelling.
Peccados adds sins to the preceding great-wickedness gloss. The doubled c is printed and retained.
Gobachi is a basin or trough used by a dyer. The Portuguese em introduces the relative clause on the next line.

runs.text: q̃ bota o tintureiro certa tinta q̃ ſe chama

lines.note: The dyer puts the preparation called Go into that basin. Both abbreviated q̃ forms remain unexpanded, and the entire embedded Go is upright rather than the draft’s mixed-font Go.

runs.text: Taboleiro de certo jogo de muitas pedras.

lines.note: Gobã is the board for the game played with many stones. The initial G corrects the malformed troba; a short worn mark above a is read as a tilde. This agrees with the Gobã identification found in the subsequent NINJAL checkpoint, but the mark is weaker than the surrounding letters.

runs.text: Sepultura de Camis, ou peßoas inſi-

lines.note: Gobeô denotes the tomb of Camis or of distinguished deceased people. The Portuguese noun has one joined ß-type pair, not the draft’s added third s; inſi- continues below. Camis is an embedded Japanese-derived term for the deities.
Gnes completes inſi-gnes, distinguished or eminent. Que morrerão refers to the deceased people whose graves are meant.
Gobeôxo is referred to the same meaning as Gobeô, the tomb or burial place just defined. Idem is the complete italic explanation.
Gobǒ is a respectful term for a bonze or religious man. The qualification Falando com is completed by reſpeito below.
Reſpeito completes the instruction to use the preceding term respectfully. The short row remains part of the monk entry.

runs.text: Hũa certa raiz como cardo, que ſe

lines.note: The second Gobǒ is an edible root compared with a thistle, not the preceding religious title. Hũa retains the printed nasal abbreviation.
Come completes the statement that this root is eaten. The small final period is visible, and no further material belongs to the row.
Gobut is a later Buddha, explained by Nochino fotoqe. The gloss’s Fotoque is an embedded Japanese-derived term; the shorter fotoqe spelling in the Japanese paraphrase is preserved independently.

runs.text: ao mũdo depois de outro ter vindo.

lines.note: The later Buddha comes into the world after another has come. The scan supports joined depois and vindo, correcting the draft’s separated de pois and viudo.
Gocacu is explained by the paired horns of an ox, Vxino tçuno, and applied to things of the same size or standing. Ameſma retains the draft’s close joining; grande- continues below.
Za completes grande-za. Gocacuno ſaburai illustrates men of matching rank or quality, with the Portuguese explanation in the next line.
The first example concerns honorable men of the same standing. Goca- starts a second example at the printed line-end hyphen.
Cuno completes Goca-cuno; buguen concerns equality in wealth and possessions. The worn b is supported by its upright and lower curve, not replaced by the r-like appearance of the damaged shoulder.
Gocai, Itçutçuno imaxime, denotes five precepts. Manda- begins the Portuguese mandamentos, continued below.

The five precepts are attributed to Xaca; V. G. introduces illustrative names. Xexxǒ is killing, followed by the injunction not to kill. Enlargement shows italic Xaca within the Portuguese gloss; it is flagged for optional whole-word font review, while Xexxǒ begins the separately glossed list.
The first injunction forbids killing a living thing. Chǔtǒ then introduces theft and its prohibition; both small carons are visible, correcting the draft’s Chitǒ.
Ras completes furta-ras. Iain is followed by the prohibition of fornication, and Vonju starts the next precept concerning drinking; these Japanese forms are retained as printed.
Vonju is explained by not drinking wine. Mǒgo then introduces false speech, whose prohibition continues as mentira below.
Mentira completes the injunction not to speak falsely. This closes the five-precept list rather than starting a new entry.
Gǒcai, paraphrased Ye vmi, denotes the sea. The initial Ye is worn but retains its capital Y and small e; the headword’s caron is visible.
Goccan means severe cold, Qiuamari ſamuxi. The doubled c and the historical ſamuxi spelling are retained.

runs.text: Penas, ou tormentos que hum recebe

lines.note: Goccu names pains or torments that a person receives. The explanation continues below to specify this life and the acts that cause the suffering.

runs.text: neſta vida pellos males, ou ruins tratos

lines.note: The torments are suffered in this life for evil acts or bad dealings. The historical spelling pellos is retained, and the relative clause specifying who does these acts continues below.
Que faz completes the reference to the evil or bad treatment that the person does. This short row closes the suffering entry.
Gochi is marked as Buddhist terminology and paraphrased as five forms of wisdom, Itçutçuno chiye. Bup. is treated as one upright label, not the draft’s internally mixed typeface; ma- begins maneiras.

runs.text: neiras de ſaber que ha no

lines.note: Neiras completes ma-neiras. The five kinds of knowing are attributed to the Fotoque; the embedded term is upright in this line.

Gǒchǒji gives a verb with zuru and ita as principal parts. Its gloss begins playing or enjoying oneself excessively. The worn word is read Brincar from the residual r/i strokes and the following folgar, not Bencar; de- begins demasiadamente.
Maſiadamente completes de-maſiadamente, followed by behaving immodestly. Inmodeſtamente is a single printed word, correcting the draft’s corrupted ending and internal gap.

Gochôxi is paraphrased as five tones, Itçutçuno chôxi, not the malformed tçitçino. V. G. introduces the list, beginning with Qiǔ; the five-count reading is supported by the visible minims as well as the gloss.
Xǒ, cacu, chi, V complete the five tone names begun with Qiǔ. The final V is visibly uppercase, and the Portuguese starts the explanation as five vocal tones.
The voice is that of a person. This closes the five-tone entry and does not belong to the subsequent royal-departure definition.

runs.text: Saida, ou ida do Rey ve-

lines.note: Gocǒ, Miyuqi, denotes a royal departure or journey. The gloss ends Rey ve-, beginning velho. Enlargement reveals a damaged undotted u between o and the dotted i of ida, so ou ida is restored rather than retaining the draft’s o ida; the u is less complete than the adjacent letters.

runs.text: lho, ou que eſta ja apoſentado. ¶

lines.note: Lho completes ve-lho. The recovered continuation specifies the old or already retired king, then begins Gocǒ, continued at the top of column 2. Most of this readable row was absent from the draft. Eſta and ja are unaccented here; the enlarged crop includes the complete initial l and the final caron.
Naſaruru completes Gocǒ naſaruru across the column boundary: his highness goes or comes out. A second example, Gocǒ na-, begins at the right and continues in the following row.

runs.text: Fazer q̃ o Rey velho ſaya.

lines.note: Xi completes na-xi; tatematçuru supplies the respectful construction. The Portuguese explains causing the old king to go out, and the abbreviated q̃ remains unexpanded.
Gǒco is paraphrased with rivers or inlets and lakes, Ye mizzu vmi. Palaura corrects the broken OCR palaara; the explanation immediately turns to metaphorical usage.

runs.text: ſe vſa no ſentido metaphorico que no proprio.

lines.note: The word is used more often metaphorically than literally. Metaphorico and proprio retain their printed historical forms rather than being modernized.

Gǒcono ſanjin is the first figurative example, glossed as a despised or disregarded person. A faint tall remnant before anjin is read as ſ, consistent with the rest of the word and the construction; the draft omitted it.

runs.text: ou de quem ſe não faz conta. ¶

lines.note: The Portuguese alternative says that no account is made of the person. A new Gǒcono example begins after the paragraph mark and continues below.
Yoriai and tçuqiai supply alternative words for a gathering or association. Ajuntamento is the Portuguese noun, correcting Ajuitamento; gen- begins gente.

runs.text: te varia. ¶ Item, As vezes pera a ba-

lines.note: Te completes gen-te, a gathering of assorted people. Item introduces a disparaging extension; the printed separated a ba- begins the verb completed below.

runs.text: ter, ſe dirà de ajuntamento de gẽte popular, ou

lines.note: Ter completes a ba-ter in the preceding row. The extension is to speak disparagingly of a gathering of common people; the grave in dirà and the abbreviated gẽte are retained.
Do Machi identifies the town or townspeople in the disparaging gloss. Machi remains italic as it appears locally, and is flagged as an embedded Japanese term for whole-word font review.

runs.text: Tempo, ou hora de madrugada, ou

lines.note: This Gocǒ denotes a time in the early morning. The final caron is faint but aligned with the repeated expression in the next row.

Antemanhãa completes the early-morning sense, followed by Gocǒno ten with the same meaning. Enlarged inspection places the tilde over the first of the two final a letters in this copy; that local evidence is retained rather than moved to fit the usual nhaã pattern.

runs.text: Rayos, ou reſplandor que pintão, ou

lines.note: A different Gocǒ denotes rays or a radiance placed around an image’s head. Rayos and singular reſplandor correct the draft’s Rijos and reſprandos; the rays are painted or otherwise applied.

runs.text: poem aos Fotoques derrador da cabeça. Ainda

lines.note: The radiance surrounds the heads of Fotoques. The initial of Fotoques is a worn capital F, not c; derrador is the printed expression for around and is not modernized.
The spelling Goquǒ is contrasted with ordinary speech. This is an embedded metalinguistic Japanese form in the Portuguese sentence, not another headword; the colon is retained.
Gocǒ supplies the spoken form that completes the preceding Portuguese sentence. Although it occupies its own short physical row, it is an embedded cited pronunciation.
Gococu is explained as five seeds or grains. The abbreviated ſ. introduces their enumeration, beginning with Co-, which continues below.
Me completes Co-me, followed by mugui, aua, qibi, and fiye. These are the five Japanese grain names; Arroz begins the Portuguese list with rice.

The Portuguese enumeration continues with wheat and barley, painço, and milho zaburro. Mugui covers the wheat/barley pair here; the historical grain names are copied without imposing a modern botanical identification.
A certain black millet or grain completes the enumeration. The text itself supplies the color rather than a precise botanical name.

Gocǒnoten refers back to gocǒ, the early-morning entry. The first o in the cited form has an abraded upper curve and can resemble u, but its rounded bowl and the cross-reference support retaining o. Vide is italic and the embedded cited form is upright.
Gocqua, Qiuamari fatçuru, concerns an ultimate or consummate outcome. The Portuguese starts with supreme good fortune, then supplies both favorable and unfavorable extremes.
Bem auenturança is blessedness, contrasted with consummate misery. The scan supports a word space after bem and e in miſeria, correcting the corrupted draft bemsuenturança and miſcria.

runs.text: pena como a do inferno, ou paraiſo.

lines.note: The extremes are illustrated by the punishment of hell and the blessedness of paradise. The visible gap in a do is retained, rather than joining it as the draft’s ado.

Gocquã denotes the highest office or dignity, paraphrased Quamaru tçucaſa. The short slightly bent mark over a is read as a worn tilde, also supported by the subsequent lexical checkpoint; Quamaru is preserved without inserting the expected i from Qiuamari above.
Nidade completes dig-nidade. The highest dignity is in the household of the Dairi, an embedded Japanese court designation whose local italic type is retained.
Gocquan is glossed Trõqueiro, a keeper of prisoners. The tilde over o represents the printed abbreviated nasal form and is not expanded.
Gocu, Nochino cu, is a final phrase or word. The adjective specifying last follows in the next physical row.
Derradeira completes the definition of a final expression. Gocuni tçumaru introduces being unable to produce a further reply, with the Portuguese explanation continued below.

runs.text: conuencido ſem poder falar mais como em

lines.note: The speaker is left convinced or confuted, unable to say anything more. The context is a debate rather than simple loss of the physical power of speech.

runs.text: diſputa, &c. ¶ Item, Não o correr a

lines.note: Diſputa supplies that debate context. Item adds failure to think of a following word or phrase; the printed o correr is kept separated rather than silently normalized to ocorrer.

runs.text: alguem algũa palaura, ou ſentença que vai

lines.note: A word or sentence fails to come to someone’s mind. The wording algũa palaura, ou ſentença and its nasal abbreviation remain intact.
The missing expression belongs to a sequence continuing with other expressions. This completes the second sense of Gocuni tçumaru.
A separate Gocu is glossed simply as rice. This is not a continuation of the preceding phrase-final sense.
Gocuacu, Togani qiuamaru, is consummate wickedness. The Portuguese cõ- begins the adjective completed in the next row.
Sumada completes cõ-ſumada, preserving the nasal abbreviation across the physical break. It closes the definition of extreme wickedness.
Gocuacunin names a person consummate in wickedness. The printed maldade is joined; the draft’s internal gap is not supported by a word-sized space.
Gocudami is illustrated by Gocudaminoye, a painting characterized by excellence. Pintu- starts the Portuguese noun, continued below.

runs.text: ra feita com perfeição, & variedade de cores.

lines.note: Ra completes pintu-ra. The painting is executed with perfection and a variety of colors; the definition itself supplies these qualities.
Gocufen is described as a vocabulary of Chinese characters. The initial of china is visibly lowercase, and the historical spelling Vocabulario is retained.
Gocufin, Qiuamaru fin, means extreme poverty. The f shapes in both the headword and paraphrase are distinct from long s, and the Japanese form is not modernized.
Gocufinna describes a person who is extremely poor. The two long-s forms in Peſſoa are preserved rather than collapsed into the joined ß-type used elsewhere.
Gocufinni is the adverb corresponding to the preceding poverty adjective. Aduer. is the complete italic grammatical explanation and remains abbreviated.
Gocugiǒ is connected with committing someone to prison, with Sadamaru fitoya as its Japanese paraphrase. The final o has a caron, and the Portuguese object follows below.
Alguem supplies the object of Prender, followed by the alternative of placing the person in prison. Carcere is copied without adding a modern accent.

Gocugiǔ is illustrated with zainin and the alternative acunin, a sinner or evil person. Both u vowels have visible carons, correcting the missing accent and grave in the draft. Enlargement confirms the detached lower-right minim of the first n in acunin, distinguishing the worn n from r.

runs.text: Grãde peccador, ou conſumado na maldade.

lines.note: The example denotes a great sinner or someone consummate in wickedness. The tilde in Grãde is retained. The separate bottom-right Go- is a catchword, not a further part of this gloss.
The isolated bottom-right Go- is a catchword in ordinary roman type. The hyphen is printed; no continuation is supplied from an unavailable following page.
